proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus is the right (ius) to alienate, destroy, or fundamentally alter a thing. In Roman-law property theory it is one of the three canonical sticks of dominium (usus, fructus, abusus). As a legally conferred entitlement it is externally grounded — the holder bears it in virtue of a social/legal recognition by the system, not in virtue of intrinsic physical constitution — which makes it a Role (BFO_0000023). It is a species of LegalRight (already in the ontology as a subclass of BFO_0000023), so Abusus subclasses LegalRight. It is a class (kind) because many individual instances can instantiate it: every Roman dominus bears their own token of abusus inhering in them.

relations.rationale: Abusus is a specific kind of LegalRight; it inherits the Role typing from LegalRight (itself typed BFO_0000023) and adds the specific legal content of alienation/destruction authority over a res.

open_questions: Should we also model the companion rights Usus (right of use) and Fructus (right of fruits) now, so that all three sticks of dominium are represented symmetrically?
Should we introduce a class 'Dominium' (Roman-law full ownership) as a composite LegalRight whose parts are Usus, Fructus, and Abusus, related via BFO_0000051 (has part)?

Is the intended scope Roman law specifically (historical individual system) or the general property-theory concept used in civil-law traditions broadly (e.g., modern French droit de disposer)? This affects whether Abusus should be an individual or remain a class.

Should Abusus be further typed as also a Disposition (BFO_0000016) on the ground that the capacity to alienate or destroy is grounded in the bearer's legal standing — or is the purely externally-granted Role typing sufficient?
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus, the ius abutendi of Roman property law, is the entitlement of an owner (dominus) to alienate, encumber, consume, or destroy the thing owned. Ontologically it is a specifically dependent continuant: it inheres in exactly one bearer (the current owner of a particular res) and cannot exist without that bearer. It is externally grounded — the entitlement arises from legal recognition and institutional status, not from intrinsic physical properties of the bearer — which places it squarely in BFO_0000023 Role rather than BFO_0000016 Disposition. Because it is a species of legally conferred entitlement, it subclasses working:LegalRight (already in the ontology as a BFO_0000023 subclass). It is proposed as a class (kind) rather than an individual because there are many token instances of abusus, one for each owner-res pair across legal history; no single unique individual is being asserted. The companion rights usus and fructus are left as open questions to keep this proposal minimal and consistent.
